title: Over a third of listed firms unable to cover interest costs: CBSL | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 03:02
-     - 0

More than a third of Sri Lanka’s listed non-financial companies failed to earn enough to cover their interest costs in the first half of 2026, as a sharp rise in revenue was eroded by higher costs and borrowing rates, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) said in a new report yesterday.

The share of listed non-financial corporates (NFCs) with an interest coverage ratio (ICR), or earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) relative to interest expense, below one rose to 37.7% from 33.8% a year earlier, the CBSL said in its Financial Stability Review 2026. The share of firms able to fully meet interest costs from earnings fell to 62.3% from 66.2%.

The assessment, based on 204 companies listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) as at end-June 2026, uses listed firms as a proxy for the wider corporate sector.

Over a third...

The deterioration came despite a strong rebound in sales. Revenue of listed NFCs grew 22% year-on-year (YoY) in 1H, up from 7.6% a year earlier, with 67.2% of firms reporting higher revenue, compared with 59.8%.

The automobile sector led the growth, with revenue soaring 138.9% following the relaxation of vehicle import restrictions, while the power and energy sector benefitted from higher energy prices amid heightened geopolitical tensions. All sectors except construction and engineering contributed positively to revenue growth.

However, aggregate net profit fell 6.1% to Rs. 137 billion from Rs. 146 billion, reversing growth of 65.2% in 1H 2025. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA), a measure of operating profit, slipped 0.4%, against a growth of 33.4% a year earlier.

Higher costs drove the decline. While revenue growth added Rs. 199 billion to profits, this was largely offset by a Rs. 152 billion rise in cost of sales, while higher distribution, administrative, and other operating costs reduced profit by a further Rs. 52 billion. Finance income and other income were insufficient to offset higher operating expenses, finance costs, and taxes.

Net profit margins and return on equity fell notably, while gross margins and return on assets also moderated. Finance costs as a share of average debt rose slightly amid higher market interest rates.

The pressure was not broad-based, the CBSL said. Median net profit and EBITDA growth remained positive, and 55.9% of firms still increased profits, marginally down from 56.4%, indicating that profit contractions at several large corporates outweighed gains among many smaller ones.

Debt servicing strain was concentrated in a few sectors. Trading and distribution recorded the lowest ICR and was the only sector unable to cover its interest costs from earnings, posting a negative net profit relative to debt. Construction and engineering carried the highest debt-to-equity ratio along with low profits relative to debt, indicating comparatively higher vulnerability. In contrast, food, beverage and tobacco and real estate recorded the strongest interest coverage, highest profits relative to debt, and relatively low leverage.

The CBSL cautioned that the simultaneous weakening of profitability and rise in borrowing costs could further constrain the debt servicing capacity of financially vulnerable firms, and that persistent earnings pressure among such corporates could lead to higher credit risk in the financial sector.

title: Yaden Laboratories makes history as first Sri Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturer to exhibit at CPHI Europe 2026 | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 03:00
-     - 0

Delegates from Guatemala with the Yaden Laboratories Management Team, representing Sri Lanka, at CPHI Milan 2026

Yaden Laboratories Ltd., a pioneering Sri Lankan manufacturer of sterile injectable pharmaceutical products, has achieved a historic milestone by becoming the first Sri Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturing company to exhibit at CPHI Europe 2026, held in Milan, Italy, from 6 to 8 October.

The achievement represents a significant step forward for Sri Lanka’s pharmaceutical manufacturing industry, highlighting the country’s growing capabilities and ambitions to establish itself within the global pharmaceutical supply chain.

Yaden Laboratories...

CPHI Milan 2026, one of the world’s largest and most influential pharmaceutical industry exhibitions, brought together an international community for which published event figures indicated over 62,000 pharmaceutical industry professionals, more than 2,900 exhibiting companies, and representation from over 166 countries.

The three-day exhibition provided a global platform for pharmaceutical manufacturers, innovators, technology providers, distributors, and industry leaders to explore strategic partnerships, emerging technologies, and international business opportunities.

Against this backdrop, Yaden Laboratories’ participation stands as a landmark achievement, placing Sri Lanka’s pharmaceutical manufacturing industry alongside some of the world’s most established pharmaceutical companies.

For the first time, a Sri Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturer established its own exhibition presence at this prestigious international gathering, demonstrating the potential of locally developed pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities to compete on the global stage.

Under the leadership of Chairman and Managing Director Shashimal Dissanayake and Chief Executive Officer Prakash Babu, Yaden Laboratories has continued to invest in advanced pharmaceutical manufacturing technologies, infrastructure, and internationally aligned quality standards.

The company’s participation reflects its broader vision of transforming Sri Lanka from a predominantly pharmaceutical-importing nation into a competitive pharmaceutical manufacturing and exporting destination.

Having established capabilities in sterile injectable pharmaceutical manufacturing, Yaden Laboratories aims to contribute towards improving access to quality-assured medicines, reducing the country’s dependence on imports and generating valuable foreign exchange through pharmaceutical exports.

The exhibition also offered opportunities to engage with international pharmaceutical manufacturers, distributors, and potential strategic partners, laying the foundation for future collaborations, technology transfers, and expansion into new export markets.

Dissanayake said: “I first attended CPHI Europe as a visitor in 2013, and since then, it has always been my ambition to see a Sri Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturing company represented at this prestigious international exhibition. 13 years later, witnessing Yaden Laboratories exhibit alongside more than 2,900 global pharmaceutical companies is an immensely proud moment, not only for me personally, but for our entire team and for Sri Lanka.”

“This achievement is the result of years of determination, investment, and the collective commitment of our dedicated team. It demonstrates that Sri Lankan companies have the capability to compete on the international stage. Our ambition extends far beyond supplying the domestic market. We want to establish Sri Lanka as a recognised pharmaceutical manufacturing and export destination, contributing to the country’s economic growth while improving access to quality medicines globally,” he added.

The achievement also reflects the collective dedication of the Yaden Laboratories team, whose technical expertise, commitment to quality, and continuous efforts have contributed towards strengthening the company’s manufacturing capabilities.

As Sri Lanka seeks to diversify its export economy and expand high-value manufacturing industries, pharmaceutical manufacturing offers considerable potential for attracting investment, generating skilled employment, advancing technology, and increasing foreign exchange earnings.

Yaden Laboratories believes that with a supportive regulatory environment, internationally aligned quality standards, and closer collaboration between Government institutions and the private sector, Sri Lanka can develop a globally competitive pharmaceutical manufacturing industry.

Yaden Laboratories’ historic participation at CPHI Europe 2026 therefore represents more than a corporate achievement. It marks an important step towards placing Sri Lanka on the global pharmaceutical manufacturing map and opening a new chapter for the country’s pharmaceutical export ambitions.

title: Data centre gap a market failure; private sector must take the lead | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 02:57
-     - 5

President’s Chief Adviser on Digital Economy Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya – Pic by Lasantha Kumara

Sri Lanka’s shortage of data centre and cloud capacity is to some extent a market failure, as clear demand from banks and other users has yet to draw private supply, forcing the Government to invest in a sector it should not need to, the President’s top digital adviser said yesterday.

“The Government really does not need to do it, but it will,” President’s Chief Adviser on Digital Economy Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya said during a conversation on digital transformation at the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit (SLEIS) 2026, moderated by The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce (CCC) Secretary General and CEO Shiran Fernando.

Demand was already evident, he said. “I think it is very clear that there is demand now. The banks are crying out for sovereign, resident cloud infrastructure.”

That demand must be matched by supply from the private sector and data centre operators, Dr. Wijayasuriya said, arguing that the gap persisted only because investors had yet to act on the supply-demand equation. 

“There are sufficient demand signals out there for supply to be created. I sincerely believe that,” he said. “The private sector can take this ball and run.”

The key barrier to resolve was the price of energy for data centres, he said. The Digital Economy Ministry is working with the Board of Investment (BOI) on an investment and incentive framework for the sector. While the Government will make some investments, its main role is to create an enabling environment for private investors, both local and new foreign direct investment (FDI), to enter the data centre, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and cloud market.

Sri Lanka’s total data centre capacity stands at around 5 megawatts (MW), against Malaysia’s 1.5 gigawatts. The country needs 25-50 MW of cloud capacity with built-in AI capability in the short term to enable AI across industries and services in both the private and public sectors, a level at which Dr. Wijayasuriya said Sri Lanka’s global competitiveness would be solid.

He cautioned, however, against unchecked expansion. Sri Lanka would take a conservative approach, targeting 25 MW in the short term given environmental concerns, and would not go as far as some regional neighbours. Malaysia had scaled up to 1,500 MW from around 5 MW in 2021, but is now pulling back after realising that data centres not serving domestic demand were effectively buying energy and selling it.

“Basically, it is an energy export. We must be very clear on the economics of that energy export and the next best use of the next megawatt generated in your country,” he said.

“We are taking a calibrated approach to ensure that our industries are legitimately competitive and that we generate sufficient export revenues from data infrastructure, while being energy sensitive and environmentally sensitive in the process,” Dr. Wijayasuriya added.

title: Reliance Consumer Products  eyes deeper Sri Lanka partnerships to expand India reach | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 02:56
-     - 0

CEO T. Krishnakumar  – Pic by Lasantha Kumara

Reliance Consumer Products Ltd., is looking to deepen partnerships with Sri Lankan businesses to take local products into India and strengthen cross-border manufacturing, sourcing, and distribution, as its top executive called for greater policy certainty and sustained investment to unlock the region’s growth potential.

Delivering the keynote address at the inauguration of the two-day Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026 organised by The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, Reliance Consumer Products CEO T. Krishnakumar said the company had built relationships with four Sri Lankan businesses over the past four years and had already launched products from two of them in the Indian market, with encouraging results.

“We value the knowledge and the capability that Sri Lankan enterprises have in many areas of consumer products,” he said, asserting the potential for partnerships that allow businesses in both countries to grow, learn, and create lasting value.

Krishnakumar said Sri Lankan and Indian enterprises could work together across product development, manufacturing, sourcing, packaging, and distribution, enabling companies to reach more consumers and build stronger regional value chains.

Sri Lanka’s established capabilities in products ranging from tea and apparel to ceramics and food offer a platform for deeper commercial collaboration, he noted, citing the longstanding cultural and economic connections between the two countries.

However, he cautioned that successful partnerships required time, mutual trust, and a commitment to sharing benefits.

“They become stronger when each partner feels heard, when commitments are honoured, and when the benefits are shared fairly,” he said.

Krishnakumar identified a predictable operating environment as a key consideration for investors making long-term commitments, noting that clarity and consistency in policy could matter more than the incentives on offer.

“Clarity and consistency, in my view, are far more important than any incentives,” he said, pointing to clear tax policies, dependable regulatory frameworks, timely approvals, and effective mechanisms for resolving difficulties as important elements of investor confidence.

He said long-term investment carried responsibilities towards employees, suppliers, and communities, making stability in the operating environment essential throughout a project’s life cycle.

Krishnakumar opined sustained dialogue between Government and industry could help build that confidence, while businesses also had a responsibility to honour commitments, provide practical feedback, and contribute to the communities in which they operate.

He said Sri Lanka had an opportunity to develop further as a regional centre for manufacturing, services, and logistics, provided the country continued to strengthen its investment environment and build on the progress already achieved.

Acknowledging Sri Lanka’s recent improvements in economic stability and reserves, he said the next phase of growth would require sustained investment in productive capacity, stronger exports, and greater opportunities for young people.

Behind the economic indicators were households, entrepreneurs, employees, and public institutions that had worked through a difficult period, he noted.

Drawing on Reliance Consumer Products’ own expansion, Krishnakumar said the company had grown from a small team of three people four years ago to nearly 11,000 employees, supported by its suppliers, distributors, business partners, and consumers.

He attributed the progress to a combination of execution, respect for local preferences, digitalisation, and affordability.

“While strategy provides direction, progress comes through the daily work of many people,” he said, highlighting the importance of maintaining quality, running efficient operations, ensuring product availability, and responding to areas that need improvement.

He also stressed that businesses entering established markets must respect local brands, consumer preferences, and cultural heritage rather than assume that products successful elsewhere would automatically succeed.

Sri Lanka’s distinct tastes, products, and consumer preferences could provide valuable insights for businesses seeking to expand internationally, he said.

Krishnakumar insisted that the consumer must remain at the centre of business decisions, with dependable quality and fair prices underpinning sustainable growth.

“I worship somebody who is the consumer,” he said, stressing the importance of understanding household needs, purchasing power, and expectations.

He pointed out that businesses must look beyond product quality alone and find ways to make quality goods affordable through better product design, sourcing, manufacturing, and distribution.

Krishnakumar also identified digitalisation and artificial intelligence (AI) as major opportunities for businesses, particularly in improving consumer access, operational efficiency, and the participation of smaller enterprises in wider markets.

Digital payments, platforms for farmers, and improved access to information could help suppliers and small businesses connect more effectively with consumers, he said.

However, he stressed that the benefits would depend on making these tools accessible and ensuring that people had the skills and support required to use them effectively.

He also said investment in talent development was equally important. Sri Lanka’s entrepreneurial capacity and young workforce offered a strong foundation, but continued investment in education, practical training, innovation, and enterprise would be necessary to translate that potential into broader economic gains.

“Businesses could contribute by investing in employees, working more closely with educational institutions, supporting smaller enterprises, and giving young professionals opportunities to take on greater responsibility,” he added.

Krishnakumar highlighted that India’s economic expansion, growing middle class, and rising consumer aspirations were opening opportunities across a wide range of industries.

Given the two countries’ geographic proximity and longstanding cultural ties, he said that closer commercial integration could benefit businesses and consumers on both sides.

He urged business leaders to view the relationship as a platform for building products, strengthening enterprises, and expanding access to markets, rather than merely increasing bilateral trade.

“Our progress is closely connected, and prosperity in either country can create opportunities for the other,” he added.

Krishnakumar said Sri Lanka’s next phase of growth would depend on sustaining confidence in its investment landscape, deepening partnerships with regional businesses, and keeping households and consumers central to economic policymaking.

“For businesses, serving consumers through affordable quality was both a commercial opportunity and a responsibility,” he added.

title: Vehicle, gold loans swell to a quarter of bank, finance company credit: CBSL | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 02:54
-     - 7

CBSL Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe – Pic by Sameera Wijesinghe

Vehicle and gold-backed loans now account for nearly a quarter of all credit extended by Sri Lanka’s banks and finance companies, as the reopening of vehicle imports and elevated gold prices fuelled a lending surge, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) said yesterday, releasing its Financial Stability Review 2026.

The two segments together made up 24.9% of total credit of licensed banks and finance companies at end-June 2026, up from 19.6% at end-2024, the CBSL said.

The share of motor vehicle-related credit, which comprises finance leases, hire purchase, and vehicle loans at finance companies together with banks’ leasing portfolios, rose to 12.9% from 9.8%. Demand built up during the import ban drove the increase after restrictions were relaxed in early 2025. Gold-backed lending rose to 12% from 9.8%, as global gold prices climbed steadily through 2025 to a record high in January 2026.

The concentration is far heavier at finance companies, where vehicle and gold-backed loans together accounted for 85.2% of total credit at end-June 2026, up from 82.6% a year earlier. Gold-backed loans alone made up 21.4%, up from 19.4%.

Finance companies’ vehicle-backed loans grew 46.3% year-on-year (YoY) at end-June 2026 and accounted for 65% of the sector’s credit expansion. Gold-backed loans grew 59.8% and contributed 25.8%. At banks, pawning grew 49.2% and raised its share of consumption loans to 37.1% from 32.1%.

The CBSL warned that such heavy reliance on two types of collateral leaves lenders exposed to falls in vehicle prices or gold prices, which have been volatile since end-January 2026. Early signs of strain are emerging at finance companies. Stage 2 loans, which are those showing a significant increase in credit risk, grew 75.5% for vehicle-backed lending and 279.2% for gold-backed lending in the year to June 2026.

CBSL Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe, however, said household debt remained below its historical average and was not yet a concern. “People are taking loans for economic activity, and only if that becomes excessive is it a problem,” he said, adding that this was why limits had been introduced for vehicle and gold-backed lending.

Dr. Weerasinghe noted that finance companies accounted for only 6-7% of total credit, although they were more concentrated in vehicle and gold-backed lending. Gold loans were commonly used for short-term working capital, particularly in agricultural areas, he said, but acknowledged that without a purpose-based classification of loans, it was difficult to determine precisely how the funds were used. Household credit data held by the Credit Information Bureau (CRIB) does not capture loan purpose and excludes gold-backed lending.

In response to the lending surge, the CBSL imposed a 70% maximum loan-to-value (LTV) ratio on gold-backed loans from 25 May. It also tightened the risk weights on gold-backed lending by banks and finance companies, removing the zero risk weight that some such loans previously carried. For finance companies, the higher risk weights took effect in September 2026. In two rounds, in November 2025 and May 2026, it cut the maximum LTV for new commercial vehicles to 60% from 80%, for other new vehicles to 40%, and for used vehicles to 60% from 70%.

The CBSL also tightened monetary policy in May. CBSL Senior Deputy Governor Dr. Chandranath Amarasekara said the impact was already visible, with private sector credit still growing in the latest month available but decelerating substantially. The CBSL expects these measures to moderate growth in both segments in the coming quarters.

Overall, the financial system remained resilient in the first half of 2026, supported by the economic recovery, improved fiscal conditions, and adequate capital and liquidity buffers at banks and finance companies, Dr. Weerasinghe said. He cautioned, however, that stability depended on sustaining the recovery, advancing fiscal consolidation, and maintaining prudent policies amid geopolitical tensions, energy price shocks, and tighter global financial conditions.

“Continued monitoring and timely policy intervention will therefore remain important in preserving financial stability,” he said.

The strain is showing in bank balance sheets. Banks’ liquidity ratios moderated as they shifted assets from Government securities to private sector lending, and short-term maturity mismatches widened. Capital adequacy ratios (CARs) declined as risk-weighted assets grew faster than capital, although buffers remained above regulatory requirements. Stage 2 loans at banks also rose in the second quarter, signalling potential deterioration in borrowers’ repayment capacity, which the report partly attributed to Cyclone Ditwah and the Middle East conflict.

The insurance sector remained adequately capitalised, though profitability moderated. Claims from Cyclone Ditwah increased reinsurance receivables and heightened underwriting, liquidity, and counterparty risks.

Domestic financial markets remained broadly stable, with the Financial Stress Index at relatively low levels. However, equity market performance moderated amid subdued investor sentiment, with weaker liquidity and higher volatility. Government securities yields rose across maturities, and foreign investor participation remained low despite a modest recovery late in the review period. The rupee came under pressure as Middle East tensions lifted foreign currency demand amid higher import and energy costs, before conditions improved on the back of policy measures and inflows from remittances, tourism, and exports.

The CBSL also flagged spillover risks from geopolitical tensions, renewed inflation, elevated energy prices, and climate-related shocks, along with rising cyber, operational, and third-party risks from the expansion of digital financial services. The outlook for financial stability remains broadly positive, it said, provided the recovery is sustained, fiscal consolidation progresses, and prudent policies continue.

On Sri Lanka’s third Mutual Evaluation of its Anti-Money Laundering, Countering the Financing of Terrorism and Countering Proliferation Financing (AML/CFT/CPF) framework, Dr. Weerasinghe said the on-site assessment by the Asia/Pacific Group (APG) on Money Laundering was scheduled for 26 October. Asked whether the country risked being grey-listed again, he said: “No. We are doing our utmost to prevent that, and we are working hard with all stakeholders to maintain our current rating and, if possible, improve it.” (CdeS)

title: Embassy in Rome promotes export and investment opportunities  at Sri Lanka Expo 2027 | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 02:40
-     - 11

The Embassy of Sri Lanka in Rome hosted a promotional event on “Sri Lanka Expo 2027” under the theme “Exploring Partnerships for a Prosperous Tomorrow” on 5 October 2026 at Circolo degli Esteri, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Club in Rome. The event brought together representatives of the Italian Government, chambers of commerce, the diplomatic corps, and Italian and Sri Lankan business communities in Italy.

The event was organised to promote Sri Lanka Expo 2027, scheduled to be held from 14 to 17 January 2027 in Colombo, and to raise awareness among Italian stakeholders of Sri Lanka’s export capabilities, investment opportunities and potential for economic and commercial partnerships.

The event commenced with the lighting of the traditional oil lamp, followed by welcome remarks by the Ambassador of Sri Lanka to Italy, Satya Rodrigo, who is also accredited to Cyprus, Greece, Malta and San Marino, and the screening of a video on Sri Lanka Expo 2027. 

The Ambassador recalled that commercial ties between Sri Lanka and Italy date back nearly two thousand years, when envoys from Sri Lanka reached the court of Emperor Claudius and Sri Lankan gems, pearls and spices were traded in Roman markets along the maritime Silk Road. He noted that Sri Lanka Expo 2027 builds on this tradition of trade and exchange and highlighted the presence of Italian companies such as Calzedonia, Intimissimi, Perfetti and Banca UBAE in Sri Lanka. He encouraged Italian businesses to further expand their engagement with Sri Lanka.

In a video message, the Deputy Minister of Industries of Sri Lanka, Chathuranga Abeysinghe, emphasised Sri Lanka’s efforts to strengthen its industrial and entrepreneurial sectors and encouraged greater engagement between Sri Lankan and Italian businesses.

The Deputy Director General for Trade and Investment Promotion of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Italy, Fabrizio Lobasso, highlighted the importance of strengthening bilateral economic and trade relations. He noted the strategic maritime locations of both countries, with Italy serving as a gateway to the Mediterranean and Sri Lanka to the Indian Ocean, and emphasised the mutual benefits of increased trade and investment.

Remarks were also delivered by the Head of Internationalization at Unioncamere (the Italian Union of Chambers of Commerce), Prof. Pietro Infante, reflecting the interest of Italian business institutions in strengthening engagement with Sri Lanka.

A key feature of the event was a virtual presentation on Sri Lanka Expo 2027 by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB) Chairman Mangala Wijesinghe. The presentation outlined the upcoming Expo and opportunities for international businesses to engage with Sri Lankan exporters and explore partnerships across various sectors. The Chairman invited Italian businesses to participate in the Expo through business delegations.

The presentation was followed by a panel discussion and interactive question-and-answer session moderated by the President of the Sri Lanka Association in Italy and Senior Product Manager at Retelit S.p.A., Rande Sarada Goonatilleke. The panel included the Ambassador of Sri Lanka to Italy, Satya Rodrigo; CNA World Honorary President, the foreign entrepreneurs’ network of Italy’s National Confederation of Crafts and Small and Medium Enterprises, Indra Perera; and the Commercial and Partnership Director of Distal GSA Italia, Claudio Novembrini. The EDB Chairman Mangala Wijesinghe, and the Minister Counsellor (Commercial) of the Consulate General of Sri Lanka in Milan, Tharaka Botheju, joined virtually.

The discussion focused on strengthening Sri Lanka–Italy trade and investment relations, promoting Sri Lankan products and services in the Italian market, and facilitating business partnerships. 

During the session, Indra Perera shared his experience in bilateral trade and highlighted investment opportunities in Sri Lanka. Claudio Novembrini explained the discounted airfares offered by SriLankan Airlines to facilitate participation in Sri Lanka Expo 2027. 

The Ambassador referred to the Calzedonia Group as an example of successful Italian investment in Sri Lanka, noting its presence in the country for over 25 years and its contribution to apparel exports and employment.

Participants sought information on investment opportunities in the food and beverage and hospitality sectors, facilities available at Sri Lanka Expo 2027, and potential partnership agreements.

The event was attended by representatives of around 30 businesses, along with Italian trade and business institutions, travel and tour operators, diplomatic missions and members of the Sri Lankan business community in Italy. A reception following the programme provided opportunities for networking and discussions on potential areas of cooperation.

The event was organised with the support of Italian Government institutions, chambers of commerce, business representatives and other partners.

The Sri Lanka Expo 2027 promotional event in Rome contributed to raising awareness of Sri Lankan products, services and investment opportunities in Italy and facilitating closer commercial partnerships between the two countries.

title: Dialog and IESL National Startup Challenge to empower entrepreneurs | Daily FT

Tuesday, 13 October 2026 02:34

Dialog Axiata PLC Head, Product and Services Innovation Chamila Wijayawardhana (right) and IESL President Eng. Kosala Kamburadeniya exchange the sponsorship agreement. Others from left IESL Entrepreneurs Forum Co-chair Eng. Nawodana Kankanamge and IESL Entrepreneurship Forum Chairperson Eng. Jasmine Nanayakkara

Dialog Axiata PLC, has joined the Institution of Engineers, Sri Lanka (IESL) to launch the IESL National Startup Challenge, creating a national pathway for aspiring entrepreneurs to transform innovative ideas into commercially viable, investment-ready startups. 

The initiative reflects a shared commitment to strengthening Sri Lanka’s entrepreneurship ecosystem through structured development, expert mentorship and practical support that enables promising ideas to progress towards market readiness and scale. 

Launched through the IESL Entrepreneurship Forum at the Dialog Auditorium on 5 October 2026, the competition invites Engineering Undergraduates, Engineering Practitioners and participants in an Open Category for Non-Engineers to submit ideas across 12 innovation verticals aligned with national priorities, emerging technology and market trends, and inclusive innovation. Participants will progress through idea development, pitching, incubation, prototyping, validation, minimum viable product development and business scaling, supported by industry experts, mentors and ecosystem partners. The program will culminate in a Top 10 selection, with the first-place winner receiving an award of Rs. 1 million.

As title sponsor and a key ecosystem enabler, Dialog is contributing practical expertise and resources beyond sponsorship, providing technical expertise, mentors and digital resources to help participating teams develop, validate and scale their solutions. Each of the Top 10 teams will also receive a Dialog Digital Startup Support Package valued at Rs. 250,000, comprising selected Dialog digital products and services.

A Dialog Axiata PLC official said: “Dialog is committed to enabling Sri Lanka’s next generation of innovators by connecting entrepreneurial ambition with the technology, expertise and practical resources needed to turn ideas into scalable ventures. Through the IESL National Startup Challenge, Dialog is extending its digital capabilities, mentorship and ecosystem support to help promising teams progress from concept to validation and investment readiness.”

IESL Entrepreneurship Forum Chairperson Eng. Jasmine Nanayakkara said: “The IESL National Startup Challenge is designed to turn innovative ideas into viable businesses by connecting aspiring entrepreneurs with industry expertise, mentorship and continuous practical support. More importantly, it is about creating an ‘Engineer to Entrepreneur’ transformation and nurturing a stronger entrepreneurial culture within the IESL community. By encouraging our engineers and aspiring founders to create, commercialise and scale solutions, we aim to contribute to new ventures, new opportunities and meaningful job creation for Sri Lanka’s skilled and educated next generation. We are grateful to Dialog for partnering with IESL to create this pathway for innovation, entrepreneurship and national economic growth.”

Driving innovation across Sri Lanka, the National Startup Challenge also brings together a strong network of partners, including The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce as Ecosystem and Mentoring Partner, Helago as Official Mobility Partner, Helakuru as Official Digital News Partner, and Real Life as Official Climate Action Partner.

The IESL National Startup Challenge represents a collaborative effort to strengthen Sri Lanka’s innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem by creating a structured pathway from promising ideas to market-ready businesses. Applications are now open via www.iesl.lk/announcements, giving aspiring entrepreneurs an opportunity to access the resources and funding they need to succeed. Applications close on 16 November 2026.

title: Dipped Products opens Rs. 4.2 b  glove plant in Katunayake EPZ | Daily FT

Hayleys Group glove maker Dipped Products PLC (DPL) yesterday said it has begun operations at its newest manufacturing facility in the Katunayake Export Processing Zone, built at an investment of Rs. 4.2 billion.

The plant began operating on 8 October, 2026 as part of DPL’s expansion plans, the company said. The facility is expected to expand DPL’s capacity to manufacture value-added gloves for export, strengthening Sri Lanka’s position in high-value rubber exports and adding to foreign exchange earnings, it said.

Robert E. Hall (left) and Michael Woodford

American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel yesterday, for work on economic stabilisation policy that underpins the models used by central banks and governments around the world.

Stanford University’s Hall and Columbia University’s Woodford developed new macroeconomic models showing that well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the peaks and troughs of the economy, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.

Central to their models is the idea that households and businesses look ahead when deciding how much to save or what prices to set. By communicating their policy plans, governments and central banks can shape these expectations about the future and steer the economy in the desired direction.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences Chair John Hassler said.

The models have since helped policymakers deal with a range of downturns, including the shocks from the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years. While recessions and bouts of high inflation have not disappeared, they now tend to be shorter-lived, the Academy said.

Hall is Professor of Economics at Stanford University and the Robert and Carole McNeil Senior Fellow at its Hoover Institution. He holds a BA in economics from the University of California, Berkeley, and a PhD in economics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and taught at both institutions before joining Stanford in 1978.

Woodford is the John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy at Columbia University. He holds a BA from the University of Chicago, a JD from Yale Law School and a PhD in economics from MIT, and has been named both a MacArthur Fellow and a Guggenheim Fellow.

The prize, worth SEK 12 million, or about $ 1.2 million, will be shared equally between the two laureates, who will also receive a diploma and a medal. It has now been awarded 58 times to 101 laureates.

Last year’s prize went to Northwestern University’s Joel Mokyr, the London School of Economics’ Philippe Aghion and Brown University’s Peter Howitt.

The economics prize was established in 1968 by Sweden’s central bank and is not one of the five original Nobel Prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace, which Alfred Nobel, the Swedish industrialist and inventor of dynamite, created through his 1895 will. The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901.

Yesterday’s announcement concluded this year’s Nobel season. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, University of Wisconsin Professor Francis Halzen won the physics prize, and Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai shared the chemistry prize. Canadian writer Anne Carson won the literature prize, while international jurist Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

The awards will be presented at a ceremony in Stockholm in December, on the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.

title: When responsible organisations remain silent | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 00:53
-     - 8

Democracy, workers’ rights and responsibility of organised society

The prevailing situation in our country calls for serious reflection and a responsible response from organised movements, particularly trade unions, professional associations and independent civil society organisations. The direction in which our laws are evolving, the exercise of governmental powers and the implications of administrative directives deserve close public scrutiny whenever they may affect democratic freedoms, social justice and the rights of ordinary citizens.

This is not merely a question of supporting or opposing a government. It is a question of recognising the responsibilities that organised society must assume in protecting the democratic institutions and freedoms upon which a just and accountable system of governance depends. Trade Unions should be partners in Social Progress.

Beyond limitations of party politics

The voice of the political opposition can often be diverted from the substance of its arguments by references to the shortcomings and failures of previous administrations. Whatever the merits of such counterarguments, the consequence may be that important questions concerning present-day governance receive insufficient public attention.

Democratic accountability, however, cannot be confined to an examination of the past. Every government must be answerable for its own decisions, legislation and exercise of public power. The shortcomings of a predecessor cannot, by themselves, justify a present measure or exempt it from scrutiny.

When conventional political debate fails to sustain attention on issues of wider public importance, independent organisations outside the party-political framework have a particularly significant role to play.

Pattern behind legislation and Government action

The concern that deserves attention is not necessarily confined to any single law, regulation or administrative decision. It is the broader pattern that may emerge when legislation, government actions and administrative directives are considered together.

A measure introduced in the name of efficiency, economic necessity, administrative convenience or national interest must be examined not only in terms of its stated objectives but also in terms of its practical consequences. What powers does it confer? What safeguards does it preserve? What avenues of challenge remain available to citizens? How might it affect the independence of institutions and organisations that have a legitimate role in questioning public authority?

These are reasonable questions in any functioning democracy. They do not imply that every government initiative is objectionable. They reflect the principle that no exercise of public power should be beyond legitimate scrutiny.

Democracy is sustained by more than periodic elections. It also requires respect for the rule of law, freedom of expression and association, institutional independence and the ability of citizens to question decisions that affect their lives without fear of arbitrary interference.

Where developments raise credible concerns about the gradual weakening of these safeguards, the public has a legitimate interest in examining them before their cumulative consequences become more difficult to address.

Why organised working class must respond

It is in this context that I wish to make my first appeal to the organised working class of Sri Lanka.

Trade unions have historically played a vital role in securing employment rights, improving working conditions and establishing collective bargaining as an essential means of protecting workers against arbitrary treatment. These achievements were not secured merely through individual representations. They depended on organisation, solidarity and the willingness of workers to defend their common interests.

Yet the conditions that make such organisation possible extend beyond the workplace.

Freedom of association, the independence of trade unions, the right to engage in collective bargaining and the ability to express grievances without intimidation depend, in turn, on a wider legal and democratic environment.

The responsibility of trade unions therefore cannot be confined exclusively to wages, allowances, working hours or individual employment disputes. When legislation or government action raises legitimate concerns about the broader rights and freedoms of working people, organised labour has a responsibility to examine those developments and express its views.

This is not a call for trade unions to become instruments of political parties. Nor is it a demand that they oppose every policy of the government of the day. It is an appeal for them to exercise their independence, assess public issues on their merits and defend the principles that enable workers to organise and negotiate collectively.

Danger of leaving vacuum in public leadership

There is another dimension to this situation that deserves equally serious consideration.

When responsible and established organisations remain silent in the face of developments affecting public rights and democratic freedoms, the consequences may extend well beyond the immediate issues at stake.

A vacuum in legitimate public leadership does not necessarily remain a vacuum for long. Where genuine grievances remain unaddressed and recognised democratic organisations fail to provide an effective channel for public expression, clandestine or unaccountable groups may seek to occupy that space. They may exploit legitimate public concerns to advance objectives that are neither transparent nor necessarily consistent with the interests of the people whose grievances they claim to represent.

This is a danger that should concern all those committed to democracy and social justice.

The answer, however, is not to suppress dissent or discourage public mobilisation. Citizens must retain their right to question authority, express dissatisfaction and demand accountability through peaceful and lawful means.

The answer lies in ensuring that credible, independent and responsible organisations remain active, accessible and responsive to public concerns. They must be prepared to articulate legitimate grievances, scrutinise government action and mobilise public opinion through transparent and democratic processes.

Silence by responsible organisations can unintentionally create opportunities for forces that do not share their democratic principles. Preventing such a vacuum is therefore not merely a responsibility of trade unions and civil society; it is also an essential contribution to democratic stability.

From individual concern to collective responsibility

The responsibility does not rest with organised labour alone. Professional associations, academic communities, independent social organisations and other representative bodies must also recognise the importance of informed public engagement.

These organisations need not share identical political views or agree on every policy question. Their common ground can be the defence of constitutional safeguards, the rule of law, institutional accountability and the fundamental rights of citizens.

They can examine proposed legislation, question administrative decisions, encourage informed public debate and seek explanations from the relevant authorities. Where legitimate concerns arise, they can make representations, engage in dialogue and, where necessary, organise peaceful and lawful collective action.

Such engagement should be based on verifiable facts, careful analysis and a willingness to distinguish genuine threats from disagreements over ordinary policy choices. Responsible scrutiny strengthens democracy; unsubstantiated allegations weaken the credibility of those who raise them.

A timely appeal

I therefore appeal to the established trade unions, particularly those representing the working people of this country, to recognise the wider implications of the present situation and consider how their collective experience, organisational strength and public standing can contribute to a constructive democratic response.

Let this also be an invitation to professional associations and civil society organisations to engage in a wider dialogue on the direction of legislation, the exercise of governmental powers and the preservation of democratic safeguards.

The objective should not be confrontation for its own sake, nor the advancement of any particular political interest. It should be the protection of the public interest through vigilance, accountability and peaceful democratic engagement.

The preservation of democracy is not the exclusive responsibility of elected representatives, political parties or public institutions. It is a continuing responsibility shared by citizens and the organisations through which they exercise their collective voice.

When democratic safeguards and the rights of working people are at stake, silence is not necessarily neutrality. It may leave important public concerns without responsible representation.

The organised working class and civil society must therefore consider not only what they stand to lose by speaking out, but also what society may lose if they fail to fulfil their responsibility.

The time has come for responsible organisations to engage with these questions openly, independently and constructively. Their intervention, guided by facts and democratic principles, can help ensure that legitimate public grievances find expression through accountable institutions and peaceful collective action.

That is not a partisan undertaking. It is a responsibility to the people, to the rule of law and to the future of democracy in Sri Lanka.

She was selected by The Gambia to sit as an ad hoc judge in its ongoing, high-profile case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya minority.

Her award has particular significance for Sri Lanka. During her tenure, the country’s internal war and its aftermath came under scrutiny at the UN Human Rights Council. Her 2013 visit to Sri Lanka, and her assessment of the rule of law, militarisation, land and accountability, informed the 2014 Council resolution mandating an international investigation. She called for credible investigations, accountability and measures to address the grievances underlying the ethnic conflict, which became a significant part of international scrutiny of Sri Lanka.  Unfortunately, seventeen years later her demands remain unfulfilled.

 At the September 2026 session of the Human Rights Council in Geneva, the Sri Lankan Government called for time limits on country specific resolutions, including those concerning Sri Lanka. This position was taken in the context of the continuation of the evidence gathering and preservation mechanism on Sri Lanka, which the Government opposes.  However, restricting the duration of international attention cannot substitute for addressing the concerns that gave rise to it. NPC urges the Government to implement recommendations made by Pillay and successive UN human rights processes which remain unfulfilled. These include credible investigations into wartime violations and enforced disappearances, protection of victims and witnesses, restoration of military occupied lands, demilitarisation of the north and east, reform of laws that undermine fundamental freedoms, and meaningful progress on truth, justice, reparations and reconciliation.

Whatever the constraints it faces, Sri Lanka, like all countries, has a responsibility to uphold these principles and fulfil its human rights commitments.

title: Stabilisation must lead to transformation;  A sovereign development fund as a way forward? | Daily FT
summary:

-     - 14

Stabilisation is retrospective; it builds firewalls around past failures, manages liquidity ratios, and enforces structural austerity to ensure a nation can barely service its liabilities. Transformation, by contrast, is prospective. It is a radical, forward-looking exercise that reimagines a country’s economic platform, moving it away from a cycle of persistent subsistence toward a high-yielding, wealth-generating future – A view expressed by development policy think tanks

Economic stabilisation achieved in Sri Lanka since its declaration of bankruptcy in 2022 is indeed welcome. All those who are responsible for this must be commended. It is imperative however to mention here that had it not been for the fiscal discipline framework introduced by the IMF, and strict adherence to it as a pre-condition set by the IMF, this recovery would not have been possible as the primary reason for the bankruptcy was in fact the absence of fiscal discipline by successive past governments. The IMF bailout therefore became a necessity rather than an option. It was the only option to prevent the country from sliding to economic oblivion. While the stabilisation process has to continue and is sustainable, it is also imperative to plan and take measures to build on the stabilised economy and transform the economy in order to ensure the debacle of 2022 is never repeated. 

Backdrop to contextualise the need for transformation

Cantered around an ongoing International Monetary Fund (IMF) Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and the newly established Public Debt Management Office (PDMO), the data from the ministry of finance and economy next reveals the following current fiscal position: 

nTotal Public Debt: $102.27 billion (approx. 95% of GDP). 

Debt Breakdown: $61.50 billion is domestic debt; $37.47 billion is central government external debt. This debt repayment is due to commence in 2028.

While above data shows a positive stabilisation position, Reuters report that Sri Lanka remains highly vulnerable to external shocks primarily on account of the country’s dependency on imports, oil and gas being the main foreign exchange guzzling imports. The IMF warns that structural fiscal stability heavily relies on sustaining energy cost-recovery pricing, continuing reform of loss-making State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), and enduring external pressures from global trade fluctuations and regional conflicts. Main commercial debt principal repayments are scheduled to resume in 2028. 

All of above, including the country’s overall debt, and in particular its foreign debt, nearly all of it accumulated over decades of bad planning and poor fiscal management, and now due to commence repayments in 2028, will add a considerable burden on the country’s still fragile economy. Its foreign reserves situation which is basically sufficient to fund imports for only a period of approximately 3.2 months and its comparatively low GDP situation, makes the country’s fiscal situation very fragile. To make matters worse for the country, the State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs), represent one of the most critical structural fiscal vulnerabilities in the country’s broader debt matrix. Recent data from the Ministry of Finance provides some data on State entity debt: 

According to official reports published by the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO), direct SOE debt accounts for roughly 3% of Sri Lanka’s total public debt

The Ministry of Finance and Economy Next have stated that while the $3.48 billion figure represents explicitly recognised debt, the structural operation of these entities presents deeper macroeconomic risks:

1.Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB): Transitioned heavily into deficits following regional weather anomalies and soaring generation costs.

2.Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC): Burdened by legacy FX debt and past subsidies.

3.SriLankan Airlines: Retains massive cumulative liabilities exceeding 600 billion rupees and deep negative equity. 

Restructuring policy 

Under the current administration, the strategy surrounding state entities has shifted. While the government has frozen previous plans to fully privatise the national carrier (SriLankan Airlines), the IMF framework legally binds the state to:

These measures have contributed to the economic stabilisation that has been achieved, but as stated, the fragility still exists due to external and internal contributing factors. While the government has introduced economic upliftment plans in the export sector, agriculture, fisheries, industrial sector, the renewable energy sector and tourism among others, it needs to look at other revenue earning mechanisms and develop a long-term plan that encompasses methods not introduced before and link some of these measures to technology, in particular artificial intelligence backed technology.

Stabilisation is not the same as transformation

When an economy suffers a systemic collapse, the immediate response of global financial institutions is to impose rigid fiscal discipline. In post-default Sri Lanka, this has manifested as an aggressive focus on revenue generation, utility tariff adjustment, and debt restructuring under the strict oversight of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Yet, an intellectual trap exists at the heart of this process: the dangerous assumption that a country can balance-sheet its way to prosperity. Stabilisation is not the same as transformation. 

To its credit, the current legislative landscape has successfully established the foundation for stabilisation. The enactment of the Public Financial Management (PFM) Act No. 44 of 2024 has brought long-overdue fiscal discipline to the state apparatus, imposing strict statutory caps on public debt, enforcing ministry accountability, and eliminating unbacked Treasury guarantees. Concurrently, the government’s 2026 Governance Action Plan aims to dismantle political patronage through the impending Public Commercial Business (PCB) Management Bill, which seeks to compel strategic state enterprises to register under the standard Companies Act, mandate cost-reflective pricing, and isolate them within a state-owned Holding Company (HoCo) 

However, in terms of transformation, while the PFM Act and the PCB Bill are significant steps toward halting financial bleeding, they remain defensive tools designed to manage state limitations and usher stability rather than inspire national growth. A holding company that merely prevents losses is still a containment strategy, not a wealth generator. To break free from this stabilisation trap over the next five to ten years, Sri Lanka must build directly upon this legislative baseline. The nation must transition from an economy that uses new laws to manage its poverty to one that uses a new financial architecture to multiply its latent worth. 

To design this future, policymakers do not need to look outward for foreign carbon-copies; they must look backward into Sri Lanka’s ancestry and how, long before the advent of modern financial parameters, ancient Sri Lanka thrived not as a subsistence economy but by its mastery of advanced hydraulic engineering, monumental architecture, strategic trade positioning, beyond hydraulic engineering, ancient Sri Lanka possessed a world-class metallurgical industry. 

The island was known in the ancient world for its iron extraction, steel production, and the manufacturing of both practical everyday implements and high-end exports. These traits are in the DNA of its inhabitants and given the right environment, they will shine as they did thousands of years ago. 

Creation of a Sovereign Development Fund (SDF)

This article proposes taking the state-owned architecture currently envisioned under the pending PCB Bill and evolving it into a modern, financialised reinsurance of that exact ancestral philosophy: drawing strength from an inward oriented, Sovereign Development Fund (SDF). Rather than keeping the proposed architecture as a passive, 100% state-owned entity, this article outlines a blueprint to structurally open it to a 51% State-owned and 49% Privately-owned equity enterprise to be set up through a Parliament Act that ensures its operational independence by requiring it to report periodically to the Parliament and not to the government. The value of private sector cash assets like bank deposits, treasury bills and bonds is estimated to be around Rs 25 trillion, and the potential for this sector to invest some component of their cash assets in the SDF is there if the SDF is able to provide a higher return to them. The private owned component should be open to investment by the Sri Lankan Diaspora as well. By operating strictly within the fiscal boundaries set by the PFM Act No. 44 of 2024, this fund will not rely on taxpayer debt or inflationary state borrowing. Instead, it will use its legislative insulation to unlock the passive rupee liquidity currently stagnant in local corporate bank deposits and convert some diaspora remittances into high-yielding, asset-backed investments.

By channelling this capital directly into AI-integrated precision agriculture, blockchain-traced marine logistics, and self-sustaining solar and wind grids, the fund aims to permanently plug Sri Lanka’s structural fiscal shortcomings. In doing so, it honours George Bernard Shaw’s timeless maxim: Some people only looking at things as they are and asking “why,” instead choosing to envision an economic platform that never was, and boldly asking, “why not? from a modernistic context. It is proposed that the SDF is structurally underpinned by some key high-tech portfolios in order to elevate Sri Lanka’s economy from a state of managed stabilisation to transformation. To this end, the proposed Sovereign Development Fund (SDF) must treat Agriculture, Fisheries, and Green Energy not as traditional livelihood sectors, but as high-yielding tech assets. By acting as the primary investor, the 51/49% fund can finance the capital-intensive deployment of among other things, Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and blockchain systems that private smallholders or a cash-strapped state cannot afford independently.

1. Agritech and Smart Plantations: Precision Yields and Direct Markets

Historically, Sri Lanka’s ancient agricultural success relied on precise, localised ecological knowledge. Modernising this ancestral strength means replacing indiscriminate chemical inputs with data-driven precision farming powered by AI.

nAI-Driven Micro-Climatic and Soil Mapping: The fund will finance a network of low-cost IoT soil sensors and autonomous drone fleets across major agricultural zones and tea/rubber plantations. AI algorithms will process real-time data on soil nitrogen levels, moisture content, and localised weather changes. Instead of blanket chemical distribution, automated machinery or targeted drones will apply precise, micro-doses of nutrients, cutting fertiliser import costs by an estimated 30–40% while maximising crop yields.

nComputer-Vision Crop Disease Detection: Mobile-based, computer-vision AI models will allow plantation managers and farmers to scan crops for early signs of blight or pest infestations. Early algorithmic detection prevents widespread crop failure, preserving premium yields of export assets like Ceylon Tea and Cinnamon.

nDisintermediation via Blockchain Marketplaces: The SDF will establish a state-backed, decentralised digital commodity exchange. By registering crops on a blockchain ledger at the point of harvest, smallholders can bypass predatory middleman layers. Global buyers can purchase directly from local farms with verified “farm-to-table” traceability metrics (carbon footprint, ethical labor, organic certification), allowing Sri Lankan exports to command a 15–20% premium in high-end Western and East Asian markets.

2. The Blue Economy and Smart Fisheries: High-Value Marine Logistics

Sri Lanka’s position on the maritime Silk Route gives it vast sovereign rights over the Indian Ocean, yet its fishing industry remains largely underutilised and inefficient. The fund will inject technology to transform fisheries into a highly scalable, sustainable export engine.

nSatellite-Aided AI Fish Finding: Deep-sea multi-day boats will be retrofitted with satellite-linked telemetry systems. Centralised AI models will analyse ocean current dynamics, sea surface temperatures, and chlorophyll concentrations to map optimal fishing zones. This eliminates blind sailing, drastically reducing fuel consumption—the largest operational cost for fishermen—and ensuring predictable catch volumes.

nAutomated Blockchain Cold-Chains: To access premium global seafood markets (such as Japan and the EU), strict temperature consistency and catch-origin data are mandatory. The fund will finance solar-powered, IoT-monitored smart cold rooms at key harbours and aboard vessels. Temperature variations will be immutably logged onto a blockchain ledger. 

nIf a shipment’s temperature fluctuates, the smart contract automatically alerts logistics managers, eliminating spoilage and ensuring 100% compliance with international biosecurity standards.

nAI Marine Sustainability Monitoring: To protect territorial waters from illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing, the fund will deploy AI-powered acoustic sensors and satellite tracking to monitor marine biomass levels, ensuring the long-term, self-sustaining preservation of Sri Lanka’s ocean wealth.

3. Green Energy: Eradicating the Foreign Exchange Drain

Fossil fuel imports represent the single largest structural leak in Sri Lanka’s national budget. Reclaiming the ancient philosophy of self-reliance means utilising the island’s year-round solar exposure and world-class wind corridors to build a digitalised, zero-fuel energy infrastructure.

nPredictive AI Smart Grids: Renewable energy (solar and wind) is inherently intermittent. The fund will finance the modernisation of the national grid into a predictive smart grid powered by AI. By analysing real-time meteorological satellite data, the AI grid can predict sudden drops in wind speed in Mannar or cloud cover over Hambantota, instantly balancing the national energy load by drawing from hydro-reservoirs or industrial battery storage.

nIoT Pumped-Storage Hydro and Battery Ecosystems: Mirroring the ancient cascading tank system where excess water was captured for later use, the fund will develop automated pumped-storage hydro installations. During peak daylight hours, excess solar energy will power IoT-controlled pumps to push water uphill into upper reservoirs. At night, this water is released to generate hydropower, functioning as a massive, natural, infinitely recyclable battery system that completely bypasses the need for imported coal or diesel generation.

nSubsea Cross-Border Smart Interconnectors: Over a 10-year horizon, as the fund expands generation past domestic demand, Sri Lanka can monetise its energy surplus. By constructing a High-Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) subsea cable across the Palk Strait, an AI-managed billing system can seamlessly export excess clean energy straight into the Southern Indian electricity grid, transforming Sri Lanka from a chronic energy debtor into a permanent, hard-currency exporter.

Conclusion

It is hoped that this proposal will gain momentum and the conceptual outline presented will provided an opportunity to consider it as a potential option to facilitate the transformation and growth of the Sri Lankan economy. The focus of the present government on digitalisation and emphasis on technology, the steps that have been taken to stabilise the economy in strict compliance with a sound fiscal governance framework, no doubt should provide an opening for this proposal to be viewed from a futuristic prism.

title: The accountability gap: Global contrasts and responses to political corruption and crime | Daily FT
summary:
