-     - 12

My Right My Decision rally United States, Salud Carbajal on Wikimedia Commons

Political accountability in a stable democracy demands that leaders in the highest levels of power are answerable to the public and are held accountable for any abuse of power by governing institutions. However, when certain states refuse to demand accountability and allow for corruption in the highest levels of power to go unchecked, it can lead to the normalisation of authoritarian leadership or practices, threatening the very fabric of democracy. With two different judicial systems and political histories, the US and Brazil reveal contrasting lessons in the value of accountability in the face of political corruption.  

Crime and punishment 

Regarded as the world’s oldest continuing democracy, the US has often portrayed itself as a global leader of democratic norms. Domestically, the US stands out as a nation with a strong representative democracy with 435 voting members of the US House of Representatives representing 802,000 people each, making it a higher representative ratio than any other democracy except India. Internationally, the US has been seen as a model for achieving democratic Government with countries like 18th century France drawing inspiration from the American experiment of self-Government for its own revolution. 

However, with the 250th anniversary of US independence, the health of US democracy seems to be in decline as the Pew Research Centre reports that the US experienced a more significant fall in democracy than other high-income democracies. In recent years, Americans have also grown less trustful of institutions, including the federal Government and major political parties. Strong democratic institutions are major cornerstones for a healthy democracy as they can enforce accountability and prevent abuses of power. Institutions are particularly crucial in achieving horizontal accountability, which is where institutions are tied to the rule of law and hold political authorities accountable when they violate the law. Several former US presidents have overstepped their presidential powers and been subjected to horizontal accountability such as Richard Nixon, who was impeached by Congress and forced to resign after ‘Watergate’ and Bill Clinton, who was also impeached by the House of Representatives for perjury and obstruction of justice linked to his extramarital affair. 

While multiple political leaders before have proven that the US is not immune to political corruption, the Trump presidency in its second term is signalling an unprecedented time in global politics for moral leadership. In May 2024, President Donald Trump was convicted of 34 felony counts of falsified business records by jurors in the New York criminal trial. Amidst an array of other legal battles, this made the president the first convicted felon to ever win a presidential election in US history, but was later sentenced to an “unconditional discharge” by a judge, removing any fine, imprisonment, or probation supervision for the president but still upholding the conviction. The moral conduct of the president has also been compared to his female political opponents, who some claim are often held to a higher moral and ethical standard. For instance, during the 2024 US presidential election, influential figures such as Michelle Obama acknowledged the double standards, stating how women like Kamala Harris are expected to be perfect, while Trump’s controversial behaviour is normalised.

The paradox of democracy is that while it can be easily dismantled, it takes years to rebuild, making one of its pillars, accountability, incredibly valuable. States like the US, with immense hard and soft power, don’t just have the ability to shape the international system but also have the ability to influence leader behaviours and political trends internationally. Hence, examples set in the US for accountability are not just pivotal for its own democratic stability, but potentially for the stability of the entire international system

Beyond personal conduct, the unilateralism of the Trump administration overseas, with President Trump acting as the commander-in-chief, has also received international condemnation and sparked conversations about the broader consequences of unchecked power. For instance, in January 2026, the illegal nature of the US capture of Venezuela’s president Nicolas Maduro was critiqued as international law prohibits the use of force in international relations except for authorisation by the UN Security Council or for self-defence. A month later, the administration’s war on Iran was also considered to be illegal by some legal experts, who claimed that there was no imminent threat posed by Iran for the US to use force or use self-defence as justification. 

In an anarchical world, it is challenging to hold world leaders accountable for their actions due to the absence of central authority, however at the state level, there are institutions available to achieve this. While some states struggle with accountability due to structural, constitutional or political reasons, other states give an important reminder that even when democracy is at its most fragile, accountability is still possible.

Protestors outside Trump’s trial in New York, Swinxy on Wikimedia Commons

Accountability v impunity 

On 6 January 2021, President Trump received his second impeachment from the US House of Representatives, for inciting an insurrection on the Capitol with the attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 US election. However, the historic impeachment trial came to an end when the president was acquitted by the Senate. This outcome was especially shocking following the prosecution case brought forward by Former US Special Counsel Jack Smith which showed evidence that the president sought to block the peaceful transfer of power, instead of accepting the election outcome. While this trial was a political process aimed at judging whether an official was upholding their oath of office or not and not a criminal proceeding, the outcome of the trial still exposed the fragility of America’s democratic traditions. A year after the Capitol insurrection, the US’s Southern American ally, Brazil, faced a similar incident as former President Jair Bolsonaro also attempted to incite an insurrection, seeking to overturn the results of the 2022 election, which he lost to his left-wing rival, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. 

Often referred to as the “Trump of the tropics”, Bolsonaro was often compared to Trump, due to similar personalities, populist far right messages and political campaigns on contentious issues. Similarly, Bolsonaro’s insurrection attempt also mirrored Trump’s as both leaders spread claims of election fraud prior to their respective elections in the effort to undermine voter trust in the electoral system. Both leaders were mobilised by online rhetoric warning of an imminent “communist” takeover of their countries. While supporters of Bolsonaro stormed the Supreme Court and pressured armed forces to intervene in support, which differed to the January 6th insurrection when Trump supporters stormed the Capitol without military intervention, both cases displayed scenes of violence and vandalism by the crowds involved. 

However, the most striking difference between these two insurrection attempts was the accountability in the aftermath. While Trump was acquitted by the Senate, Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years in jail in 2025 by the Supreme Court after being found guilty of plotting a coup.

Political accountability in a stable democracy demands that leaders in the highest levels of power are answerable to the public and are held accountable for any abuse of power by governing institutions. However, when certain states refuse to demand accountability and allow for corruption in the highest levels of power to go unchecked, it can lead to the normalisation of authoritarian leadership or practices, threatening the very fabric of democracy

This leads to the question – why was one state successful in their accountability while the other not?

The main reason is Brazil’s institutional resilience by the Federal Supreme Court and the Supreme Electoral Court. The Brazilian Supreme Court, consisting of a panel of five justices, has the authority to preside over criminal charges against high level political officials. Hence, the five member panel led by Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes voted to convict Bolsonaro on all five charges which include attempting to orchestrate a coup, directing an armed criminal organisation, and seeking to violently dismantle Brazil’s democratic rule of law. Brazil’s 1988 Constitution played a major role, as it established the Judiciary’s independence by restricting “interference by the armed forces, whether official or semi-official according to Brazilian politics”. Therefore, it guarantees that politicians like Bolsonaro cannot undermine democratic institutions. In comparison, while the US Supreme Court also tries cases involving high-level officials, they provide more presidential immunity, thereby shielding presidents from legal accountability. For instance, in the case of Trump vs United States the Supreme Court ruled that presidents have an absolute immunity from prosecution from core official acts, citing the separation of powers doctrine embedded in the constitution as the reason. Conservative Judge John Roberts, who made the presidential immunity ruling, was known to issue ‘Trump-friendly rulings’, demonstrating the impact of partisan judicial decision-making. While law experts claim that politics has always played a role in decision-making, the parties themselves are becoming more polarised and judicial ideologies more contentious, thereby changing the dynamics of the court. 

Additionally, Brazil also has a fragmented political party system, where 24 political parties are represented in the Brazilian National Congress. Due to this fragmentation, it is difficult for a single party to win a majority in an election, encouraging coalition building. This multi-party system varies significantly to the two-party system in the US, where the parties, the Democrats and Republicans, are in opposition, increasing the likelihood of political polarisation and resulting in a legislative deadlock on contentious issues. For instance, the Democratic-controlled US House of Representatives passed the vote to impeach Trump, making it the most bipartisan vote on a presidential impeachment in history. However, the Republican-controlled Senate ultimately voted to acquit the president, underscoring the deep divisions within the US political system. This differed to the fragmented Brazilian right, represented by at least four parties in Congress, who were not particularly in favour of Bolsonaro.

Former President Jair Bolsonaro in the gallery, while the Supreme Court ministers hand down their judgment Gustavo Moreno/ STF on Wikimedia Commons

However, Brazil’s model of democracy is far from perfect, as the country continues to face various threats. Certain scholars claim that after Bolsonaro’s trial, politics in the nation has become increasingly polarised, resembling US politics, as many far-right figures have strongly opposed the ruling by the Brazilian Supreme Court. This polarisation is also visible in their National Congress since a conservative-majority Congress approved a bill in April 2026 to reduce the jail sentence of Bolsonaro, making his sentence fall from 27 years and three months to 22 years and one month, if confirmed by the Supreme Court. Alongside polarisation, political dynasties are another significant threat to a democracy, as it erodes the chances of fair and equal electoral representation for non-dynastic politicians. Hence, political dynasties in Brazil continue to be prevalent with the son of Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro, launching his campaign for the October 2026 presidential election. Mirroring his father’s trajectory, Flavio Bolsonaro is also facing a corruption scandal over the unlawful financing of a film about his father, which is negatively affecting his polls ahead of the election. 

Despite these recent developments, the democratic achievements of Brazil have not been undermined, as the country has proven to show resilience even during turbulent political eras, shaping the outcome that made Brazil’s accountability successful today. 

Court trials and tribulations

In 1964, the right wing armed forces overthrew the democratically elected president, Joao Goulart, resulting in a military dictatorship rule from 1964 to 1985 in Brazil. During this period, the military junta implemented Institutional Acts which included dissolving the National Congress, suspending elections and the censorship of media. However, after a period of economic instabilities and anti-establishment campaigns such as the Diretas Jar campaign, the election of Jose Sarney influenced the drafting of the 1988 Constitution. The 1988 Constitution embedded strong judicial independence, facilitated democratic elections, and introduced transparency mechanisms forming Brazil’s modern accountability framework. 

Brazil’s political history has enabled not just the development of systems to protect democracy, but also embedded a memory in its citizens that helps recognise signs of authoritarianism which trigger urgent action. Alternatively, other states such as the US who lack experiences with authoritarian leadership domestically might overlook the same signs.

There have been a series of events in US history that resembled authoritarian practices. For instance, the McCarthy era involved the brutal targeting of individuals who were suspected to be supporters of Soviet Union Communism. This resulted in mass job losses and blacklisting. According to Amnesty International, Government repression has been considered as an authoritarian practice. Furthermore, the Jim Crow era, which marginalised African Americans, could also be described as an authoritarian practice due to its brutal prosecution of those who defied the Jim Crow laws.

Significant gains have been made in the effort to enforce accountability in the US which echo similar trends in the other regions such as South Asia. In recent years, anti-Government protests have erupted across the region. Most recently, the Cockroach Janta party protests in India have mobilised millions of young people against the Modi Government over criticisms that the Government was not taking responsibility for the medical exam leaks that affected millions of students

However, due to the US constitutional order that has historically ensured civilian control over military rule, experiences of a dictatorship have been unlikely in the US making the signs of democratic backsliding less prominent. Instead the US has shown interest in overturning authoritarian rule internationally, such as the toppling of Muhammar Gaddafi’s regime in Libya and most recently, the Iran war, which also aimed for regime change. Alternatively, US support for the Brazilian military’s anti-communist interests during the Cold War, showed that the US also supported military dictatorships overseas, particularly when it aligned with their ideologies. 

Despite authoritarian histories, if the past fails to resonate and institutions fail to implement change, accountability may have to depend on other influential actors. 

No one is above the law 

Vertical accountability, another type of accountability, refers to the process by which voters discipline those in power. Although this is primarily executed through elections, protests may also be an effective way to execute this accountability. The right to protest is especially important for a healthy democracy as seen with the Diretas Jar movement, as it can call out injustices and especially demand change for a better future. The US in particular has seen strong mobilisation efforts by the citizens to protest the actions of President Trump and his administration. The No Kings Protest in March 2026, meant to be an anti-authoritarian rally protesting the Trump administration, was recorded to include the greatest number of protests in a single day in US history, with a number of 3,300 events happening across the country. The protests drew people across various issues, from the administration’s ICE raids and war in Iran to the leadership of Trump himself.

Events leading up to the 1964 coup, Arquivo Nacional on Wikimedia Commons

Hence, significant gains have been made in the effort to enforce accountability in the US which echo similar trends in the other regions such as South Asia. In recent years, anti-Government protests have erupted across the region. Most recently, the Cockroach Janta party protests in India have mobilised millions of young people against the Modi Government over criticisms that the Government was not taking responsibility for the medical exam leaks that affected millions of students. Calls for accountability have shown success, as India’s Education Minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, has since resigned, proving the important role of the people in achieving accountability. 

The paradox of democracy is that while it can be easily dismantled, it takes years to rebuild, making one of its pillars, accountability, incredibly valuable. States like the US, with immense hard and soft power, don’t just have the ability to shape the international system but also have the ability to influence leader behaviours and political trends internationally. Hence, examples set in the US for accountability are not just pivotal for its own democratic stability, but potentially for the stability of the entire international system. 

(The author is a third-year Arts student specialising in International Relations. She is particularly interested in feminist foreign policy, international defence and security and developments in US and Middle Eastern politics. She is also passionate about analysing global topics through an intersectional lens in her writing)

title: Beyond better buses: Future of public transport in Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 00:04
-     - 15

LMT Kadawatha MetroLink Depot via LinkedIn

The launch of Lanka Metro Transit (LMT) marks a genuine milestone. Set up as a subsidiary of the Sri Lanka Transport Board and approved by Cabinet in 2025, LMT began as a modest pilot in April 2026: ten low-floor, air-conditioned buses running two routes, Makumbura–Fort and Makumbura–Kadawatha, imported under the ‘Clean Sri Lanka’ initiative. Within months, it had expanded rapidly - new depots under construction, over a hundred additional Foton buses arriving, and a plan to grow from two routes to seven, reaching well beyond Colombo’s core. For a country that has spent decades talking about mass rapid transit without much to show for it, seeing steel, depots, and dedicated fleets materialise is worth celebrating.

But the more interesting question isn’t whether LMT is a good project. It almost certainly is. The question is whether it represents something bigger than a single infrastructure upgrade - whether it could be the first move in a genuine rethink of how Sri Lankans move within its commercial capital and beyond.

Sri Lanka is not starting from zero. Few countries of its size have such extensive existing coverage: a bus network that reaches almost every corner of the island, and a rail system with real historical depth that was once used to bring commodities from across the island to the Port of Colombo. On paper, the skeleton of a strong public transport system is already there.

The problem has never really been coverage. It has been coherence. Buses, trains, and three-wheelers largely operate as separate worlds rather than one system. Congestion in Colombo continues to worsen, and research has linked inadequate transport infrastructure to a meaningful drag on national output. Reliability is inconsistent enough that most people who can afford an alternative choose one. Integration (the ability to move seamlessly from one mode to another) remains the exception rather than the rule. 

The LMT will not fix any of this on its own. Its real significance will depend on what surrounds it. 

Learnings from a recent visit to Vietnam

Looking at the public transport systems in the Vietnamese cities of Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, what strikes isn’t just a single piece of infrastructure; it is how connected different modes of transport were.

The new metro lines in both cities still have limited reach, but they are clean, frequent, and clearly built with future expansion in mind. Buses are everywhere, and while they don’t always feel modern, they run often enough that waiting for one doesn’t feel like a gamble. To ensure continuity, ride-hailing platforms have slotted in to fill the gaps. Booking a ride or a delivery is fast, prices are transparent, and it functions as a real extension of the transport system rather than a substitute for one.

Motorcycles yet remain the dominant mode of transport, and that has real costs; visible in the noise, the density of traffic, and the sheer discipline required to cross a street in central Hanoi. Certain pockets, particularly around the Old Quarter and newer commercial districts, are genuinely walkable, with short blocks and active street life that make getting around on foot pleasant rather than an afterthought. Intercity connectivity also felt considered: domestic flights between Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City are frequent and affordable, and the highway network connecting major economic centers has visibly improved even in the last few years.

I want to be careful here. Countries like Vietnam are not a transport utopia. Congestion is real, motorcycle dependence carries safety and environmental costs, and much of the mass transit network is still years from maturity. The biggest takeaway isn’t ‘perfection’. It is the sense that every piece, imperfect as it is, seemed to be built with an eye toward how it connects to everything else.

Lesson 1: Think networks, not projects

The single biggest lesson is this: LMT cannot succeed as a standalone project. It has to be conceived as one node in a much larger network - connected to existing rail lines, the wider SLTB bus fleet, hubs like Makumbura and Kadawatha, the three-wheelers that handle first- and last-mile trips, and the BRT/LRT/MRT corridors envisioned in the longer-term Colombo Metropolitan Transport (CoMTrans) master plan published by JICA in 2014.

Encouragingly, the early signs suggest planners understand this. Makumbura and Kadawatha are being developed as multimodal terminals rather than isolated bus stops, and Borella is emerging as a central hub knitting several routes together. But a network on a map is not the same as a network a commuter actually experiences. Think of any journey as a chain: home to feeder transport, feeder to mass transit, mass transit to an interchange, and interchange to final destination. 

A commuter doesn’t experience “the metro bus” in isolation. They experience the whole journey. 

Therefore, a journey is only as good as its weakest link. A fleet of a hundred and seventy new buses surrounded by unreliable feeder services and chaotic interchanges will still lose passengers to private vehicles, because the failure point isn’t the bus. It now becomes everything around it.

Lesson 2: Make public transport a choice, not a necessity

Sri Lanka has long treated public transport as an essential service for those without other options; which is a legitimate and important function, but an incomplete ambition. A modern system needs to go further: it needs to attract people who own a car or a motorcycle and could drive, but make the conscious decision not to.

That shift requires taking reliability, frequency, comfort, real-time information, easy payment, and overall journey time just as seriously as affordability. This is where Vietnam’s ride-hailing applications come into play. Ride-hailing doesn’t compete with public transport; it makes the whole system more convenient and affordable, which is precisely the standard private car owners are quietly comparing everything else against.

Lesson 3: Transport infrastructure moves an economy

This is perhaps the most consequential lesson, and the one most often missed in transport debates that focus narrowly on buses and trains. Mobility determines who can reach which jobs, which universities, and which markets. A reliable 45-minute commute puts a far wider range of employment and opportunity within someone’s reach than an unpredictable two-hour journey, even if the physical distance is identical.

In this sense, transport quietly redraws a country’s economic geography. It determines which parts of a city or region can meaningfully participate in economic growth, and which remain effectively cut off despite being only a short distance away on a map. Investment in public transport is investment in labour markets, business competitiveness, and productivity; not simply in convenience.

When Cyclone Ditwah struck Sri Lanka in late November 2025, it caused the worst flooding and landslides the country had seen in over two decades. Transport infrastructure absorbed a disproportionate share of the damage. Of the World Bank’s estimated $ 4.1 billion in direct physical losses, infrastructure - roads, bridges, railways and water networks, accounted for the largest single share, at $ 1.735 billion. 

Sri Lanka’s railway network was especially hard hit, with only around 478 of its 1,593 kilometers of track left operational in the aftermath, cutting off entire parts of the island from the rest for weeks. For ordinary commuters, this meant journeys that were already unpredictable became impossible. For the tourism sector, already a vital source of foreign exchange, damaged roads and severed rail links to the hill country and east coast compounded the disruption at exactly the time visitor access mattered most. The episode is a stark illustration of the argument at the heart of this piece: transport is not a convenience layered on top of the economy. It is the connective tissue the economy depends on, and when that tissue tears, the costs ripple through labour markets, businesses and export earnings alike.

Lesson 4: Develop places, not just corridors

The final lesson is about ambition. The most successful transit systems don’t just move people - they shape the places around them. Transit-oriented development treats stations and multimodal hubs not as pass-through points but as genuine economic nodes: surrounded by housing, offices, retail, and services that give people reasons to arrive, stay, and work, not just transfer.

That raises a genuinely exciting question for Sri Lanka. What could Makumbura, Kadawatha, or the country’s major railway stations become if transport planning and urban planning were treated as a single problem rather than two separate ones? I believe LMT gives Sri Lanka an opening to answer that question properly; but only if the ambition extends well beyond the tracks themselves.

Public Transport Depot, Ho Chi Minh City

LMT: Buses are only the beginning

Perhaps the most important takeaway is not something Sri Lanka should copy from other countries. It is a different way of thinking about transport itself.

Developing countries are often tempted to measure infrastructure progress through visible assets: kilometers of road built, buses purchased, railway lines rehabilitated, or stations opened. LMT itself could easily be measured this way - by the number of buses deployed, routes opened, or passengers carried. But its real value should be judged by something much bigger: what does LMT allow people and businesses to do differently?

Can someone living outside Colombo use an LMT connection to reach a railway station and access a better-paying job without spending several hours commuting? Can Makumbura or Kadawatha become gateways through which businesses access a wider labour market? Can a passenger move from an SLTB feeder bus to LMT, rail and finally a three-wheeler without having to plan each leg as a separate journey? And when floods, fuel shortages or other disruptions occur, can an integrated network provide alternative ways of keeping people moving?

Those are ultimately questions of mobility, not buses.

And this is where LMT could become far more consequential than its initial scale suggests.

Sri Lanka does not need LMT to become another transport system operating alongside the systems it already has. It needs LMT to become the connective layer between them. Its routes and hubs could provide the backbone around which existing buses, railways, three-wheelers and eventually BRT, LRT or MRT services are progressively integrated. Common ticketing, coordinated timetables, real-time journey information, well-designed interchanges, and reliable feeder connections would arguably matter just as much as expanding the fleet itself.

That also means thinking differently about the infrastructure surrounding LMT. Makumbura, Kadawatha, and future hubs should not simply be places where passengers change buses. With the right planning, they can become economic nodes around which offices, retail, housing and services develop and extend economic activity beyond Colombo’s traditional center, while giving people access to opportunity without necessarily owning a car.

This is the larger opportunity LMT creates.

Its success should therefore not simply be that more Sri Lankans ride better buses. Success would be fewer people feeling that purchasing a private vehicle is the inevitable price of economic progress. It would mean businesses accessing larger pools of workers, regional communities becoming better connected to employment and education, transport hubs attracting investment, and Colombo gradually becoming a city where mobility does not automatically mean more vehicles on already congested roads.

When visiting countries like Vietnam, it leaves travellers with the impression of a country increasingly treating connectivity as part of its development strategy rather than merely as a transport problem.

LMT allows Sri Lanka to begin doing the same.

The new buses arriving in Sri Lanka are important. But whether LMT becomes a successful bus service or the beginning of a genuinely different mobility system will depend on everything we choose to connect to them.

(The writer is an engineer, project management professional, and energy and infrastructure development enthusiast with experience across engineering, project development, and business strategy. He can be reached at jadrianjansz@gmail.com)

Mohamed Salah has set a new record in Turkiye’s top flight of club football, becoming the first player to have 10 goal contributions in his first seven games for Trabzonspor in the Turkish Super Lig.

The Egyptian icon provided an assist in Trabzonspor’s 3-0 win over Samsunspor on Saturday and took his goal-assist tally to three in addition to his seven goals in as many fixtures in a prolific start to his career in Turkiye since his move from Liverpool.

The 34-year-old joined the Turkish side from the English Premier League club in August on a two-year contract in what was then seen as a surprise move.

Salah was a free agent after leaving the Anfield club at the end of the last season in English football.

When his move to Trabzonspor was completed, Salah was greeted by throngs of fans on his arrival in Istanbul.

The Egypt captain made his competitive ⁠debut for ⁠Trabzonspor off the bench in their Turkish Super Lig season opener against Kasimpasa, which ended in a 1-1 draw.

A month later, he scored a hat-trick and provided an assist as Trabzonspor thrashed defending champions Galatasaray 4-0 at home, handing the Istanbul side their first defeat of the season.

Lionel Messi said his farewell to ‌the Argentina national team earlier this week when he played his final match for the three-time world champions, ending a 21-year international career.

Messi’s next task will be to break Inter Miami out of their five-match winless streak in Major League Soccer (MLS) when they host DC United on Saturday.

Manchester City shrugged off the threat of sanctions to beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 in their first game since being found guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules.

Second half goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki on Sunday extended City’s flawless start under Enzo Maresca after Ryan Gravenberch had been sent -off for two yellow cards.

Victory reestablishes City’s three-point lead at the top of the table, but the future of any title challenge rests on the outcome of the club’s appeal against widespread financial impropriety.

An independent commission found City and their Emirati owners arranged “sham” deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.2bn) between 2009 and 2018.

No sanction has yet been handed down, but a severe points deduction or even expulsion from the English top-flight is on the table unless City overturns the decision.

There has even been speculation that there could be retrospective action to strip City’s titles.

The multiple breaches of Premier League laws came during a period in which City won three titles and a clutch of other trophies.

City’s rivals believe, however, that the illegal spending during that period also built the foundations for a golden era under former boss Pep Guardiola, who left at the end of last season.

Liverpool were one of the clubs most affected, having finished second to City three times in the past 12 years.

“There are so many moments and memories we can’t get back,” Liverpool fan Martin Reilly, 23, told the AFP news agency. “They have to throw the book at them.”

City arrived under the protection of a police escort with a hostile Anfield welcome expected, but there was no repeat of the violent scenes when their team bus was pelted with bottles ahead of a Champions League clash in 2018.

Liverpool fans lined the streets to greet the visitors with chants of “cheats” and “going down”, while merchandise stalls were littered with flags and scarves mocking City’s financial scandal.

In the iconic Kop end behind one goal, a banner read “a generation of supporters cheated”.

The battles between Guardiola’s City and Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool in recent years became the Premier League’s marquee event.

But with the eyes of the world watching today, Liverpool failed to rise to the occasion on the field.

New Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola’s options were blunted without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo as the Spaniard suffered his first defeat since taking charge of the Reds.

The home side briefly flickered into life at the start of the second half when Lewis Koumas was denied a goal on his first Premier League start by Gianluigi Donnarumma.

The Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008 transformed City from mid-table mediocrity into the dominant force of the English game.

City’s economic might was on full display to help turn the game, as Maresca could turn to Jeremy Doku off the bench early in the second half.

Within minutes the Belgian winger had been chopped down by Gravenberch, who was shown a second yellow card and Liverpool never recovered.

Doku’s deflected shot was then smashed home by Haaland to break the deadlock 25 minutes from time and open the floodgates.

Three minutes later Doku curled a sensational strike into the top corner himself.

Cherki then exchanged a slick one-two with Josko Gvardiol before slotting under Alisson Becker to rub salt in Liverpool’s wounds.

City midfielder Elliot Anderson told reporters after the game that his side had shown “courage” as they got the win in a hostile atmosphere.

“We have shown togetherness and fight, this is tough place to come and we have shown courage,” he said.

“It [the noise from the Anfield crowd] was more than normal … Arriving and the first 10 minutes of the first half, but we quietened the crowd and improved in the second half.

“During the game you can feel it, and it is a game where you have to stick together and we did.”

title: Ajith Wijayasinghe receives Asian Badminton Meritorious Award | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 00:00
-     - 5

Badminton Asia General Manager Kenny Goh (right) presenting the Meritorious Service Award to Ajith Wijayasinghe at an event in Indonesia

Ajith Wijayasinghe was honored by Badminton Asia as the recipient of the prestigious Meritorious Award in the Technical Category in recognition of his immense contribution to developing technical officials, both local and international, over the years.

He recalls the journey with pride and recounts the ups and downs he endured during this period with his traditional humility.

A product of Richmond and Wesley, he was introduced to the game at the age of 11 by the father of Badminton in this country, the late Ariyadasa Silva, who was Master-in-Charge of Badminton at Richmond College. But as fate had designed, at the age of 14 his parents decided to migrate to Colombo and Ajith was admitted to Wesley College in 1966.

Badminton, which had flourished at Wesley in the late ’50s and early ’60s, had declined to non-active status, and the revival of the game took place in 1967 when an enthusiastic group led by Shanthi Macleland, Ranil Senevirathne, Kingsly Nallathamby and a couple of others brought it back as a recognised sport in the school. Ajith, being a player from Richmond, was automatically in the Squad.

This group had regular training in the College Hall and by the late ’60s and early ’70s was a formidable team. They brought honors to the school at Inter School Tournaments and National Level Events. By early 1970 they had already planned the succession in training juniors, among whom players of the caliber of Malik Jahn and Sarath Basnayaka, who later became national champions, were groomed.

In 1972 Ajith became Junior National Champion in Sri Lanka.

Ajith, along with Kingsly Nallathamby, who was already National Champion of Sri Lanka, continued to coach the youngsters. Ajith had chosen Badminton Coaching as his vocation and strove to develop in this field. He underwent a Badminton Coaches Training Program conducted by a Chinese Expert, Tang Xehua, in 1979 while still a player in the National Badminton Squad.

He was appointed to the Executive Committee of Sri Lanka Badminton in 1979 as Assistant Treasurer, a position he held till 1980, when he was appointed General Secretary of Sri Lanka Badminton under the Presidency of the late P. Sivalingum.

The period 1980–1982 was a remarkable one for Sri Lanka Badminton, as the proposed construction of a dedicated Stadium for Badminton was pursued very positively under the dedicated commitment of the late Dr. R. Vigneshwaran. This dream became a reality in 1982 when the Buildings Department finally completed the construction and the present Stadium at Maitland Place was declared open.

The SLBA immediately started training players at National Level and the National Junior Squad, and commenced a Coaching School for beginners, making use of the stadium facility to its full potential. Ajith pursued his Coaching Ambitions and was among the first batch of coaches in the SLBA Coaching School while also serving as a backup coach for the National Senior and Junior Squads.

In 1986 Ajith was nominated to attend a Coaches Training Program conducted by the International Badminton Federation in Thailand.

He also realised the importance of activating the Mercantile Sector, which possessed tremendous resources that could help the game and its top players in the future. He pursued this ambition with the assistance of a dedicated team which included Eraj Wijesinghe, the late Ananda Alahakoon, the late Raja Molligoda, the late S.J. Weerasena and the late Themuth Jayathunga, and in 1982 the Mercantile Badminton Association was inaugurated and officially recognised as a Sectoral Affiliate of Sri Lanka Badminton.

Ajith received his first International Award in 1997, when the International Badminton Federation conferred on him the IBF Meritorious Award. Up to this point in his career, Ajith had no intention of becoming a Technical Official.

However, as destiny designed it, the 1983 Civil Unrest, which had been a major setback for every activity in the country, affected Sports as well. Against this background, there was a general appeal from the Ministry of Sports to invite foreign teams to visit Sri Lanka. The MBA, which was headed by Eraj Wijesinghe, embarked on conducting an International Badminton Event in Sri Lanka, and this was the turning point for Ajith to take on a new role in the area of technical and event organisation.

In 1985 a steering committee comprising Eraj Wijesinghe, Raja Molligoda, Major S.J. Weerasena, Ananda Alahakoon, Vijitha Perera, T.P. Jayathunga and the late Eva Kodithuwakku took over this herculean task. Most countries politely declined the invitation, as Sri Lanka was listed as an unsafe destination for tourists. However, confirmations were obtained from 05 countries, mainly through personal contact and persuasion. This was a major success, and the team was energised to go forward.

With this success in hand, a suitable location had to be developed to conduct such an event, as there was no Sugathadasa Indoor Stadium at that time. Under the determined leadership of Major S.J. Weerasena, Vijitha Perera, Raja Molligoda and Ajith, the structure, which was the trolley bus garage and popularly known as the Indoor Stadium, was upgraded to a suitable standard to host an International Badminton Event. 

The next major hurdle was the Technical Officials, as Sri Lanka did not have anyone qualified. With the help of the late Dr. A.R.L. Wijesekara, 8 former National Badminton Players were groomed as Umpires and Service Judges for the Tournament. The rest of the technical requirements were handled by Ajith in his capacity as Organising Secretary. 

The event was titled the John Player International Badminton Championships Sri Lanka, and Ceylon Tobacco Company along with the Maharaja Organisation were sponsors for the event.

It was after 16 years that an International Badminton Event was held in Sri Lanka, and it was a tremendous success by all standards.

Ajith was immediately recognised for his capacity as an Event Organiser and Technical Official. This began his journey in the technical arena, and he started conducting regular training of potential technical officials, many of whom are today Internationally Accredited. He was appointed as a Trainee Referee of the IBF, and his first International Assignment was the Iran Fajr Championships in 1987.

Ajith was conferred the status of International Referee in Badminton in 1997 after an evaluation conducted by BWF officials. His major role was to develop Sri Lanka’s Technical Officials, which he undertook with great commitment over the years.

As an International Referee, Ajith has officiated in over 50 countries at events at all levels. His wide experience was rewarded with appointments such as Chief Referee of the Commonwealth Games in Melbourne, Chief Referee of the All-Africa Games in Nigeria and Competition Manager at the Asian Games in Doha.

Ajith retired from Refereeing in 2019 after serving over 30 years as an Active Referee and today functions as a Referee Assessor for Asia. He continues to serve Sri Lanka Badminton in every way possible.
